articles.title: A Rhode Island family planned more than 200 affordable apartments on 31 acres; the town seized the site for a municipal complex after a $775,000 appraisal, but a federal judge later voided the taking
articles.summary: A federal judge has blocked the Town of Johnston, Rhode Island, from taking control of a 31-acre property planned for affordable housing.
articles.body: A federal judge has blocked the Town of Johnston, Rhode Island, from taking control of a 31-acre property planned for affordable housing. The judge ruled that town officials did not have the legal authority to seize the land. US District Judge Melissa R. DuBose overturned the town's decision to take the property near George Waterman Road. The ruling clears the way for the Santoro family and their development company, SCLS Realty LLC, to continue plans for a 252-unit housing complex. The decision ends a major legal dispute between town officials and property developers over land rights, local zoning rules and state requirements for affordable housing.Secret condemnation and social media discoveryThe dispute began when the Santoro family submitted plans to build a large residential development on their 31-acre property. Under Rhode Island law, developers can avoid certain local zoning restrictions if a town has less than 10 per cent of its housing classified as affordable. Johnston's affordable housing share stood at about 7.9 per cent. To stop the proposed development, the town government, led by Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr., moved to take the property through eminent domain. This legal power allows governments to acquire private land for public use under certain conditions. Town officials said the land was needed for a combined municipal complex that would include a new police headquarters, fire department headquarters and town hall. In early 2025, the town filed the condemnation paperwork, deposited an appraisal amount of $775,000 in a state court registry and transferred the property's title to the municipality. According to legal filings in SCLS Realty, LLC v. Town of Johnston, documented in court records and reported by the Washington Examiner, town officials completed the transfer without notifying the owners beforehand. The Santoro family learned that the property had been seized only after seeing an announcement posted by town officials on social media.Legal action and constitutional challengeIn March 2025, SCLS Realty LLC filed a federal lawsuit against the town. The company was represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation and local legal counsel. It argued that the seizure was unconstitutional and amounted to an unlawful taking of private property. According to reports by Rhode Island Current and The Public's Radio, the lawsuit accused the town of creating its own condemnation process, breaking open meeting laws and claiming a public purpose to delay the housing project. The Pacific Legal Foundation criticised the move as a "sham taking". The organisation argued that town officials had used their eminent domain powers to get around Rhode Island's affordable housing requirements. Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr. rejected claims that the town had acted in bad faith. Speaking to local media, he said the planned municipal complex was the main reason for the land acquisition. "No, it's about building the complex," Polisena Jr. told The Public's Radio. "I mean, that is the number one priority. I don't think there's anything more quintessential to a municipal government than providing public safety." The Rhode Island Attorney General's office later reviewed the town's initial actions and found that the town council had violated the state's Open Meetings Act during its early votes on the land acquisition. The council held another vote in March 2025 to approve the condemnation again. However, the developers continued with their federal lawsuit, seeking to overturn the seizure altogether.Court strikes down municipal overreachIn a ruling issued by the US District Court for the District of Rhode Island, Judge Melissa R. DuBose sided with the developers and declared the town's seizure of the property invalid from the beginning. The court found that Johnston officials had failed to follow the legal procedures required to use eminent domain. Judge DuBose ruled that local governments cannot create their own condemnation systems to avoid the legal protections that apply when private property is taken. The decision prevents the town from relying on the invalidated process to take control of the land. "This ruling reins in the Town's obvious abuse of power and protects every American whose land a government might decide it wants," said Kady Valois, an attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, in a statement released after the court's decision.Impact on local housing mandatesThe court's ruling restores ownership of the 31-acre property to SCLS Realty LLC, allowing the Santoro family to move forward with its plans for the 252-unit housing development. The decision could have wider effects across Rhode Island, where several towns have struggled to meet the state's requirement that at least 10 per cent of their housing stock be affordable. Legal experts working on land-use issues say the ruling shows that local councils cannot use land seizures to avoid state-backed housing requirements. Johnston officials indicated after the ruling that they might consider other legal options concerning the property. However, the federal court's order prevents the town from interfering with the site through the eminent domain proceedings that have been declared invalid. The future of the proposed housing complex will now depend on the next steps taken by the developers and any further lawful action pursued by the town.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2002, Japan widened a 70-metre road using crushed oyster shells in its base; testing found the shell section exceeded the ground improvement target
articles.summary: Discover how Japan transformed seafood waste into a sustainable solution for road strengthening, showcasing positive results from a unique 2002 engineering experiment with crushed oyster shells.
articles.body: Discarded oyster shells are often associated with seafood waste, stockpiles and the challenge of finding storage space. In parts of Japan, oyster-farming shells became the focus of a practical engineering experiment. Rather than sending the material for disposal or using it only in agriculture, researchers investigated whether crushed shells could help strengthen the ground beneath roads.According to a study published in the Journal of the Society of Materials Science, Japan, crushed oyster shells were tested in a Japanese road-widening project in March 2002, with the trial covering a 70-metre stretch. Researchers monitored the road’s response to traffic using pavement deflection measurements and found that deflection decreased over time. The section containing nearly dry oyster shells also achieved an estimated California Bearing Ratio above the target set for ground improvement. The findings suggest that discarded oyster shells may be useful for strengthening road subgrades, although further testing is needed under different conditions.Why Japan was looking for a use for discarded oyster shellsThe experiment aimed to address a practical problem in oyster-producing areas. After oysters were removed, the shells would pile up in storage yards. Some of these would be used again as an additive to animal feeds, fertilisers, and soil conditioners. This method of using shells did not always keep up with production levels. Piling up shells caused problems in terms of occupying space and creating foul odours and worsening the environment. Using these shells for crushing purposes presented an alternate solution. The crushed shells would be used for making better roads.The approach was not entirely untested. A study published in Doboku Gakkai Ronbunshu in September 2002 examined the suitability of crushed oyster shells for road subgrades through laboratory experiments and simulated ground-improvement tests. The researchers found that incorporating roughly 20% crushed shells could improve the ability of construction equipment to travel over the treated ground and could contribute to the effectiveness of soil stabilisation. The study suggested that the small, irregular shell fragments could perform well beneath asphalt pavements. The next experiment moved the research outside the confines of the laboratory. Rather than depend only on the results of laboratory testing on samples, the engineers were able to see the performance of the material after the road had been built.What happened after vehicles began using the road?The researchers used a falling weight deflectometer to measure how much the road surface bent under a controlled load, helping them assess the pavement’s strength without digging into it. The Society of Materials Science, Japan also reports that maximum deflection at the loading point tended to decrease during the monitoring period, suggesting the pavement resisted bending more effectively under the test conditions. The best results came from the section containing nearly dried oyster-shell fragments, where the estimated California Bearing Ratio (CBR), a measure of soil strength and resistance to penetration, exceeded the target set for ground improvement.These findings suggested that oyster-shell fragments could be a useful alternative in the road-widening project, but they did not establish that shell powder or other forms of oyster-shell material could replace conventional road materials in every situation. Further testing under different soil and weather conditions, along with longer-term monitoring, would be needed to determine how well the material performed over time.Could seafood waste become a regular road material?The significance of the Japanese study lay in its practical approach to waste management. Rather than sending discarded oyster shells for disposal, the researchers tested whether the material could serve a useful purpose in road construction. The 70-metre trial produced encouraging results for the ground supporting the pavement, but it did not establish that oyster shells could be used directly as a road-surfacing material. The study also did not quantify the long-term cost savings or establish how the material would perform under different conditions over many years. Nevertheless, it showed that locally available shell waste could meet a specific ground-improvement target under the conditions tested.The March 2002 project provided a field-based assessment of oyster-shell fragments as a construction material, moving beyond the idea of waste reuse to examine their performance under real road conditions. Its findings offered evidence for a potential use in areas with substantial quantities of discarded shells, while leaving questions about durability, wider applications and long-term economic benefits unresolved.You use AI every day. articles.title: In Cameroon’s black-cotton-soil road experiment, researchers mixed bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime into the ground; its bearing score rose from 2.7% with bamboo charcoal alone to 19% with the final mixture
articles.summary: Discover how researchers in Cameroon have combined bamboo charcoal, quarry dust, and lime to significantly enhance the load-bearing capacity of Black Cotton Soil, paving the way for durable roads in challenging conditions.
articles.body: Building durable roads on weak soil is costly, particularly in regions where the ground swells when wet and shrinks as it dries. In Cameroon, researchers tested whether bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime could strengthen Black Cotton Soil, an expansive soil that can weaken road foundations.According to a study published in the International Journal of Civil Engineering, the researchers examined how combining the three materials affected the soil’s load-bearing capacity. The best-performing mixture, containing 20% bamboo charcoal, 12% quarry dust and 5% lime, increased the soaked California Bearing Ratio (CBR) from 2.7% to 19%. The laboratory results suggested that the combination could improve the suitability of this difficult soil for road construction, although its performance under actual road conditions would require further assessment.Why Black Cotton Soil creates problems for roadsBlack Cotton Soil contains large amounts of clay and changes volume as moisture levels vary. In wet seasons, Black Cotton Soil absorbs moisture and swells. When it dries, it tends to shrink and form cracks. These changes can strain road foundations and deform the road surface. The problem is especially serious when the subgrade, the prepared earth beneath the road, is made of Black Cotton Soil.The research explains that bamboo charcoal was first used as a soil amendment to alter the soil’s engineering properties. The researchers tested several charcoal proportions and selected the 20% bamboo charcoal mix for further analysis. The selected mixture achieved only a 2.7% soaked CBR. That led the researchers to test other substances that could improve the mixture. Lime and quarry dust were added in sequence to enable the scientists to observe the impact of each substance on the bearing capacity of the soil. This approach matters because soil stabilisation involves more than simply adding one material to the soil.How quarry dust and lime improved the mixtureQuarry dust is a fine material produced during rock crushing. When added to the bamboo-charcoal-treated soil, it helped improve the mixture’s bearing capacity. The addition of lime produced a further increase, bringing the soaked CBR to 19%, more than seven times the value recorded for the charcoal-only mixture. The researchers also found that the soil’s Plasticity Index fell to 11.2%, indicating a reduction in its plasticity.These results are consistent with other studies on stabilising expansive soils. A study published in Construction Materials found that chemically stabilising black cotton soil improved its engineering properties, highlighting the importance of selecting suitable additives. However, the Cameroon experiment’s results came from laboratory tests and do not guarantee the same performance on construction sites, where soil composition, drainage, rainfall and compaction can vary. Further field testing would be needed to establish how reliably the mixture performs under real road conditions.Could the mixture be used in road construction?The Cameroon experiment was notable for combining three materials to improve the strength of difficult soil. Bamboo charcoal offered a potential use for processed bamboo, while quarry dust provided a way to reuse a by-product of stone processing. Lime, already used in soil stabilisation to modify plasticity and improve soil properties, formed the third part of the mixture. The significance lay in testing how these materials worked together, rather than assuming that any one additive could deliver the same results on its own.For road builders, the approach could be useful in areas where expansive soils are common and conventional ground improvement is expensive. However, its practical value would depend on the cost of producing and transporting bamboo charcoal, the local availability of quarry dust and the amount of lime required. The environmental impact of charcoal production would also need to be considered.Further field trials would be necessary to establish how the treated soil responded to repeated traffic loads, wet and dry cycles and changing groundwater levels, as well as whether the mixture could be prepared and compacted consistently at construction sites. Although the researchers reported a substantial increase in bearing capacity under the tested conditions, its performance and cost-effectiveness in wider road-building applications would require further assessment.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mike Tyson and wife Lakiha sued in £1.5 million High Court battle over Rabona sponsorship deal after alleged refusal to film giant talking pigeon video; boxer denies breach of contract
articles.summary: Mike Tyson and his wife, Lakiha Tyson, are embroiled in a £1.5 million High Court legal battle in London over claims that the former heavyweight boxing
articles.body: Mike Tyson and his wife, Lakiha Tyson, are embroiled in a £1.5 million High Court legal battle in London over claims that the former heavyweight boxing champion unlawfully withdrew from a lucrative marketing campaign after objecting to a promotional video featuring a giant talking pigeon. According to a report by The Independent, Medier Ltd, the company behind online gambling brand Rabona, is suing Tyson and his promotional business, Tyrannic, alleging breach of a sponsorship agreement signed in January 2024. Tyson and Tyrannic deny the allegations.The dispute centres on an agreement under which Tyson was to promote Rabona’s gaming services through live-streaming events and other promotional activities. The contract reportedly involved a $2 million fee, payable to Tyrannic in instalments, of which nearly $190,000 was paid before the relationship broke down.As reported by The Independent, Medier alleges that Tyson and Tyrannic failed to participate in agreed live-streaming events and terminated the contract without proper notice.Barrister Ali Reza Sinai, representing Medier, told the court that Tyson and his company effectively walked away from the agreement after he secured a much more lucrative deal to fight YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul.Describing the Netflix-backed exhibition bout as the “elephant in the room”, Sinai argued that Tyson and Tyrannic had lost interest in the Rabona arrangement once the fight was confirmed.“The defendants simply lost interest in the service agreement once the more rewarding exhibition fight was firmly agreed,” Sinai said in written submissions. He also argued that fulfilling the sponsorship obligations had become inconvenient for Tyson and his company.Giant talking pigeon at centre of legal disputeAt the heart of the disagreement is a proposed promotional video called ‘Talking Pigeons’, which Tyson’s legal team says went well beyond what had been agreed under the sponsorship contract.According to the court submissions detailed by The Independent, the concept required Tyson to interact with four presenters, including one dressed as a giant pigeon. The boxer was allegedly expected to participate in scripted role-play, answer questions, share childhood stories and teach the presenters how to box.The proposed segment also involved a mannequin bearing the face of Tyson’s former opponent, Evander Holyfield, which the presenters were expected to punch. Tyson would then play casino games on the Rabona website while interacting with them through a video link.Medier’s legal team maintains that Tyson and Tyrannic failed to honour their contractual commitments. The defence, however, argues that the proposed entertainment format was never part of the performance Tyson had agreed to provide.Tyson’s lawyers say promotional demands exceeded contractBarrister Amanda Hadkiss, representing Tyson and Tyrannic, told the court that the requested performance went “far beyond the scope of what might reasonably be considered to have even been required” under the agreement.She argued that the contract limited Tyson’s filmed activities to playing casino games, including slots, poker and roulette, or participating in other games and events featured on Rabona’s website, provided those activities had been approved.The defence contends that the ‘Talking Pigeons’ concept was fundamentally different from the activities specified in the contract.Hadkiss said Tyson was not contractually required to take part in the proposed show and argued that Tyrannic had therefore not breached the agreement by indicating in advance that he would not attend or by his subsequent non-attendance.The High Court will have to consider the competing interpretations of the sponsorship agreement as the hearing continues.Jake Paul fight and Amsterdam event add to disputeThe court heard that Tyson’s exhibition bout against Jake Paul was initially scheduled for July 20, 2024, although it eventually took place in November that year. Tyson lost the contest, which was streamed on Netflix.Under the Rabona agreement, Tyson was also expected to attend a promotional event at a major gambling conference in Amsterdam scheduled for July 16 to 19, 2024.Medier’s barrister argued that Tyson and Tyrannic may have been concerned that the Amsterdam appearance could conflict with restrictions under the Netflix agreement, which allegedly limited non-fight-related sponsorship activities during the build-up to the bout.Sinai argued that there was a “clear and significant risk” that the defendants could be viewed as breaching the Netflix agreement if the Amsterdam sponsorship event was advertised and went ahead.The defence disputes that Tyson’s withdrawal amounted to a contractual breach, maintaining that the nature of the requested promotional performance itself exceeded the agreed obligations.Mike Tyson’s lifelong love of pigeonsThe dispute has an unusual connection to one of Tyson’s best-known personal interests: his lifelong affection for racing pigeons.As noted in The Independent’s report, Tyson has frequently spoken about his love for the birds and their importance during his difficult childhood in New York. In his autobiography, he wrote about how caring for pigeons became a meaningful part of his early life.He has also recounted an incident in which a man killed one of his pet pigeons, an experience he has linked to his first involvement in physical confrontation.Tyson became the youngest heavyweight world champion in boxing history in 1986, at the age of 20. Known for his explosive power and aggressive fighting style, he later retired with a professional record of 50 victories and seven defeats.The current dispute is not about Tyson’s affection for pigeons itself, but about whether the proposed pigeon-themed promotional show fell within the obligations he had accepted under the Rabona agreement.The High Court hearing is continuing. No finding of liability has been made against Tyson or Tyrannic.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Who is Najmeh Amini? Iranian accounting student facing death sentence over social media post
articles.summary: Najmeh Amini, a 23-year-old Iranian accounting student, faces a death sentence for alleged blasphemy linked to a social media post. The case highlights the Iranian government's crackdown on dissent following nationwide protests.
articles.body: An Iranian accounting student has been sentenced to death on blasphemy charges over a social media post.Najmeh Amini, 23, is being held at Vakilabad prison in Mashhad, north-eastern Iran. She has received a death sentence in one case and a prison term of 12 years, six months and one day in another, according to The Guardian.The case comes amid a wider crackdown following nationwide protests in January, during which thousands of people were reportedly killed. According to the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested during the crackdown.What are the charges against Najmeh Amini?A source close to Amini’s family told the US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRAI) that she was sentenced to death on a charge of sab ol-nabi, as cited by The Guardian.Amini was reportedly arrested after Iran’s Cyber Police, known as Fata, monitored her online activity. The specific content of the social media post has not been made public.In a separate case, she was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day in prison on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the government.Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, reported that Amini told the court she had made the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends. Her defence described the incident as a “slip of the tongue”.The presiding judge reportedly rejected the explanation, questioning why Amini had not insulted other individuals or opponents of the Iranian government while in the same state.Under Article 262 of Iran’s Islamic Penal Code, insulting the Prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. Article 263 provides exemptions in certain circumstances, including where the remarks were made without deliberate intent.What did Amini say in her appeal for help?An audio recording attributed to Amini and released last month contains an appeal for international intervention. She called on the United Nations, lawyers and human rights organisations to investigate her case.“I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice,” she said.In the recording, Amini also spoke about her hopes for the future and the distress her situation had caused her family.“I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams,” she said, adding that her parents were waiting for her and feared losing her.Her appeal has added a personal dimension to concerns raised by rights groups over the death sentence and its implications for online expression in Iran.Why are human rights groups concerned?Rights organisations have warned that Iranian authorities are increasingly using executions to intimidate the public and suppress dissent.Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO) reported that more than 600 executions had already been carried out in Iran this year.Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, the organisation’s director, said Amini’s sentence risked extending the use of capital punishment to peaceful expression. He also warned that the Iranian authorities were testing how far the international community would tolerate such cases.Death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively uncommon in Iran despite the recent rise in executions. The last documented executions in blasphemy-related cases took place on May 8, 2023, when Yousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executed after convictions linked to social media activity.You use AI every day. articles.body: The US needs roughly 1.7 million new skilled workers annually through 2035, according to The State of America’s Skilled Trades report. Yet the Trump administration has tightened restrictions on foreign workers, including suspending eight technology and outsourcing firms from filing new applications under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, according to The Times of India.The contrast highlights the challenge facing the US as it seeks to meet growing demand for skilled workers while prioritising domestic hiring.The report, backed by Jobs for the Future (JFF) and the Burning Glass Institute (BGI), says the US workforce system is preparing only 55 qualified workers for every 100 needed across key technical fields.It estimates that 24% of the skilled trades workforce is aged 55 or older, raising concerns about retirements and replacement needs. Demand is also growing amid investments in data centres, energy modernisation and advanced manufacturing.Industrial machinery mechanics and millwrights rank at the 98th percentile on the national Labour Shortage Index, while electricians rank at the 85th percentile.The report points to a widening gap between the number of skilled workers required and the workforce being prepared to meet that demand.PERM suspension affects major technology firmsThe US department of labour suspended eight technology and outsourcing firms from filing new PERM applications. The affected companies include Indian IT firms Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Cognizant, as well as US companies Microsoft and Adobe.PERM is a key step in the employment-based green card process for many foreign workers, including some H-1B visa holders. The reported suspension has added uncertainty for Indian IT professionals seeking permanent residency through employer sponsorship.US officials cited concerns about wage undercutting and alleged misuse of foreign-worker programmes. The administration has said its aim is to encourage companies to hire American workers.A test for US workforce policyThe two developments present a challenge for US workforce policy. The skilled-trades report points to a substantial shortfall in the domestic pipeline, while the immigration crackdown seeks to reduce reliance on foreign workers.Whether domestic training and recruitment can meet the projected demand of 1.7 million new skilled workers a year through 2035 remains a key question.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1956, a 60-year-old California woman found building blocks too expensive and began hauling bottles from a dump; 25 years later she had turned tens of thousands of discarded objects into a 15-building folk-art village
articles.summary: When Tressa Prisbrey was 60 years old, she wanted to build a small shed for her large pencil collection.
articles.body: When Tressa Prisbrey was 60 years old, she wanted to build a small shed for her large pencil collection. In 1956, she found that concrete blocks cost more than she could afford. Rather than give up, the California resident began collecting thousands of discarded glass bottles and household items from a nearby landfill. Over the next 25 years, she turned a one-third-acre lot in Simi Valley into Bottle Village, a well-known folk-art site with 15 structures, shrines, mosaic paths and sculpture gardens. According to historical records kept by Preserve Bottle Village, the non-profit organisation that looks after the site, the project began soon after Prisbrey and her husband parked their trailer on Cochran Street. After buying the land, she had little money left for building materials, so she turned to a local dump to find glass bottles.Constructing structures out of landfill scrapsSoda bottles usually had a two-cent deposit, so people rarely threw them away. Prisbrey instead collected discarded milk of magnesia bottles, alcohol bottles and other glass containers. She mixed mortar by hand and placed the bottles horizontally in the walls, with their bases facing outwards. The glass allowed natural light to pass through, creating colourful patterns inside the structures. From 1956 to the mid-1960s, Prisbrey built 15 separate structures, each with a single room. Official site records show that three were called Pencil Houses, where she displayed thousands of pencils. Other buildings included the Doll House, which held more than 600 dolls she had rescued from being thrown away. Once she ran out of space to build more structures, Prisbrey began decorating almost every available part of the property. She made mosaic paths from broken tiles and crockery, created a headlight garden from old car parts, and built shrines using seashells, horseshoes and discarded household items.Art born from grief and showmanshipFolk-art experts and art historians see Bottle Village as both a personal memorial and a remarkable creative achievement. Prisbrey outlived six of her seven children, and she built several parts of the site to remember family members she had lost. Records published by Preserve Bottle Village explain how her personal experiences shaped specific structures. She built the Shell House in just two days after learning that one of her sons was critically ill. The Heart-shaped Shrine was dedicated to her daughter Velma. Although many of the structures were linked to painful events, Prisbrey brought humour and a natural flair for entertaining visitors to her work. As news of the unusual site spread, Bottle Village became a popular local attraction. Prisbrey led daily walking tours and charged visitors admission fees ranging from 25 cents to one dollar. When people asked about her methods and how she worked without standard building materials, Prisbrey gave a straightforward answer. She believed creativity mattered more than money. "Anyone can do something with a million dollars. Look at Disney. But it takes more than money to make something out of nothing and look at the fun I have doing it," Prisbrey remarked in statements recorded in the project archives.Critical acclaim and historical preservationPrisbrey never considered herself a professional artist, but her work gained wider attention in the art world during the 1970s. In 1974, architectural critic Esther McCoy discussed the site's cultural importance in an essay for a catalogue published by the Walker Art Centre in Minnesota. "At the root of her uniqueness is a divine disorder; she has a passion for all discarded objects and shows a willingness to provide them all, equally, a place in her scheme," McCoy wrote in her analysis of Prisbrey's work. Bottle Village received official recognition in 1981, when it was named California State Historical Landmark No. 939. It was later designated a Ventura County Cultural Landmark and a Simi Valley City Landmark. In 1996, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places. Prisbrey moved to San Francisco in 1982 because of her declining health. She died in 1988 at the age of 92. Ownership of Bottle Village had been transferred to Preserve Bottle Village in 1986. The site received further recognition in 2025, when it became an affiliate member of Historic Artists' Homes and Studios. The national programme is managed by the National Trust for Historic Preservation and recognises places connected to artists and their work.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: TNSTC bus breaks down near Muthupettai in Tiruvarur; students and public push it aside to clear traffic amid rain, sparking criticism over maintenance.
articles.body: Tiruvarur: A Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation (TNSTC) bus broke down on the road near Muthupettai in Tiruvarur district on Wednesday, forcing school students and the public nearby to push the vehicle to the side to prevent a traffic pileup. articles.title: ‘Jatayu’ returns to Amherst Row through Sukeas St puja theme
articles.summary: Sukeas Street Durga Puja in Kolkata honours actor Santosh Dutta’s birth centenary with a Jatayu-themed pandal recreating scenes from Satyajit Ray films.
articles.body: Kolkata: On Sukeas Street, a neighbourhood puja working within modest means but competing fiercely in imagination, has turned nostalgia into its strongest material. Its theme this year is Santosh Dutta, the actor whose comic timing, expressive face and unmistakably Bengali mannerisms made him one of the most-loved figures in Bengali cinema.The tribute comes on Dutta’s birth centenary. Born on Dec 2, 1925, in undivided Bengal, he came to live in the neighbourhood, at 49, Amherst Row, when he was seven. Known as Suradhwani Kutir, the house remained his address for life. For organisers, that local connection makes the tribute intimate rather than ceremonial.“For many in the neighbourhood, Dutta is not just a cinema artiste but a resident who used to walk the streets and have tea at local stalls. In life, his persona was very different from that on screen: he was serious and rarely cracked jokes,” recounted Sibendu Mitra.The pandal treats the theme like a walk through Bengali memory. Using sculpture, painted frames, light, shadow and installations, it recreates moments from Dutta’s life and screen presence. Old Kolkata lanes, a theatre stage and the suggestion of a film set appear in layers, allowing visitors to move through spaces that evoke both the city and the cinema that shaped him.Dutta’s association with Satyajit Ray forms the installation’s emotional centre. Ray brought him from theatre to cinema, and the pandal marks that turning point through ‘Parash Pathar’, his debut film. From there, it invokes ‘Teen Kanya’, ‘Mahapurush’, ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne’, ‘Sonar Kella’, ‘Jana Aranya’, ‘Joi Baba Felunath’ and ‘Hirak Rajar Deshe’ through character studies, symbolic props and stylised tableaux.A key attraction is Lalmohan Ganguly, or Jatayu, the thriller writer from ‘Sonar Kella’ and ‘Joi Baba Felunath’. Dutta made Jatayu more than comic relief, giving him warmth, fear, vanity, innocence and loyalty.“I have drawn heavily from ‘Joi Baba Felunath’ and the character Lalmohan Babu who uses the ‘chadmanaam’ or pen name of Jatayu. We have tried to recreate the Ghoshal family house thakurdalan showcased in the movie. Since space is limited, we have used the balconies of the Srimani Bari as part of the thakurdalan installation,” explained artist Indrajit Ray, adding that a golden Ganesh has been kept inside the lion’s jaw just like in the film. The Idol-maker Bablu Paul was asked to make the idol resemble those seen in bonedi baris in the 1970s. The tribute also recalls Dutta’s “Researcher” in ‘Hirak Rajar Deshe’, Abalakanta from ‘Ogo Bodhu Sundari’, and his association with Gopal Bhar. Together, they underline his place in Bengali wit, folk humour and satire.The Sukeas Street puja refuses to treat comedy as lesser art. It presents Dutta’s humour as observation, rhythm and emotional truth. Dutta, who died on March 5, 1988, returns here as a cherished “Parash Pathar” — a touchstone of laughter, mystery and memory.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.summary: Madras High Court seeks reports on PIL urging free battery-operated cars for disabled, seniors and pregnant women at all Madurai & Trichy railway stations.
articles.body: Madurai: Madras high court on Wednesday directed the Centre and Southern Railway to file reports on a plea seeking a direction to provide battery-operated cars free of cost to persons with disabilities, senior citizens and pregnant women in all railway stations under the Madurai and Trichy railway divisions.A division bench of Justice P Velmurugan and Justice K K Ramakrishnan was hearing a public interest litigation filed by Swamimalai Sundara Vimal Nathan of Thanjavur district.The petitioner stated that battery-operated cars are provided at railway stations as a mobility-assistance facility to help senior citizens, persons with disabilities, pregnant women and other needy passengers reach or leave their coaches, particularly since the distance between platforms and coaches allotted for persons with disabilities is usually positioned at the extreme ends of trains.He stated that this facility was introduced for free in Trichy Junction in 2017. articles.title: ​A New Zealand couple bought an abandoned school, then spent three years and about NZ$250,000 turning the classroom into a home and chalet; the property is now listed for enquiries over NZ$595,000
articles.summary: For years, an old school sat quietly on the edge of Tokanui, a small township in Southland. Then Ian ‘Hippy’ Rogers and his wife, Sue, arrived.
articles.body: For years, an old school sat quietly on the edge of Tokanui, a small township in Southland. Then Ian ‘Hippy’ Rogers and his wife, Sue, arrived. They took one look at the school and saw something most people didn’t. The couple knew the neglected property had the potential to become a home.The school at Quarry Hill first opened in the late 1800s, although the building the couple bought dated from 1958. It closed in 1993, and subsequent owners had done little with the property.In 2017, when the couple arrived, hedges had swallowed much of the site. But they weren’t ready to give up. They invested a couple of years in turning the school into a home. Now, the property is on the market for enquiries over NZ$595,000, according to a report by Trade Me Property.Two ways of looking at a ruinWhen the couple first laid eyes on the dilapidated building, they saw two things. Sue saw what it could become, while Ian saw the work it would take. Sue admits the decision required some persuasion.“I wouldn’t say we agreed instantly. It was more a wife nagging,” Sue told the outlet.Ian laughs when he remembers it. “She was looking at it, going, ‘This will be wonderful’, and I was looking at it, going, ‘Look at the work involved’.”Before they knew it, they were looking at a long-abandoned schoolhouse, a derelict outdoor swimming pool and changing rooms that were almost swallowed by the hedges.Sue had always wanted to renovate a school, although she admits people look at her strangely when they discover her day job. She’s a school principal. “We’d been looking for something unusual. We liked renovating, so my random idea was to find an old school in Southland.”Renovation beginsBefore any walls could be touched, the couple had to clear the land. Thirty years of hedges, weeds and wildlife had taken over the half-hectare block. They worked with Invercargill builder Craig Brown, and the school was stripped back to its framing. New insulation was installed, and most of the windows were retrofitted with double glazing. Luckily, the building’s structure was in good condition. “Structurally, it was already about 90 to 95% sound,” Ian said.A new 9.6-metre beam was installed above the kitchen and lounge to support part of the rear wall and a small extension. They reused original materials wherever possible.A school that still feels like oneSue wanted the house to retain its past. “It had to feel like a fun school,” she said. She chose the colour palette, giving the school a bold and quirky look. “It’s still got the character and the history of the school within the building.”Some original details survived the renovation. For instance, a giant chalkboard hangs above the bed, and the cubby holes where generations of students once left their school bags are still there.Pool turns into chaletAnother part of the renovation was the pool, which was badly damaged when the couple bought the property. It had to go. “It could have become a nursery, a big glasshouse or a veggie garden,” Sue added. But they kept coming back to a beach-themed chalet that could serve as short-term accommodation. The main building took about three years to finish. The one-bedroom retreat inside the former pool came later.The renovations cost the couple an estimated NZ$250,000. That figure excludes their own labour and is slightly higher than Sue’s initial estimate.The property is now listed for enquiries over NZ$595,000 through JJ Morgan at Bayleys. The couple is ready for their next project, and Sue already knows what she doesn’t want. “Not an old school!” For now, she is done with schools.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: ‘Custody death victim was tied up with lungi’
articles.summary: CB-CID chargesheet names 11 accused in Nagercoil sub-jail custodial death case; alleges disabled inmate Sabarivarman was tied with a lungi and assaulted.
articles.body: Kanyakumari: The CB-CID chargesheet in the custodial death of a 34-year-old disabled inmate inside Nagercoil sub-jail in July reveals that the accused tied the victim’s hands and legs with a lungi before intensifying the assault.When the victim, Sabarivarman, managed to free his hands, the accused became furious, tore the lungi, tied him up again and continued the assault, which resulted in his death, the investigation further revealed. The accused include prison warden Jagan, chief warden Suresh, prison guard Sivakumar, and eight inmates.CB-CID has filed a chargesheet against 11 people before a Nagercoil court in connection with Sabarivarman’s custodial death at Nagercoil district prison.Sabarivarman, a petty shop owner from Eethankattai near Suchindram, was arrested by Thenthamaraikulam police on July 9 for possessing 200 grams of gutka. Remanded to judicial custody, he died on July 13. A case was registered by Nesamani Nagar police, and eleven, including eight prison inmates and three jail wardens, were arrestedAccording to the CB-CID investigation, a prison warden first assaulted Sabarivarman after inmates complained that he was shouting inside the cell and insisting on meeting his wife and children. Investigators said the warden later instigated eight inmates returning from kitchen duty to attack him again. The probe found that the accused tied the victim’s hands and legs with a lungi and repeatedly assaulted him.The family of the victim had held a roadblock outside Kanyakumari Govt Medical College and Hospital with his body, demanding compensation from the govt. articles.title: 100+ detained as students, MPs march to Jantar Mantar
articles.summary: Over 100 detained near Jantar Mantar as SFI-DYFI and Youth Congress march, target CEC Gyanesh Kumar, and oppose protest-site denotification and voter roll issues.
articles.body: New Delhi: Over 100 people were detained near Jantar Mantar Tuesday after student and youth outfits held two separate marches towards the iconic site.Both demonstrations echoed similar slogans, including “Jantar Mantar wapas karo” and “Gyanesh Kumar isteefa do”. Those detained included two CPM MPs from Kerala: A A Rahim and V Sivadasan.Both marches took aim at CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter rolls and a recent order issued by MHA denotifying Jantar Mantar as a protest site.Ayan, one of the protesters, said, “They have scared us so often that we have now stopped fearing them.” At around 1.35 pm, he and other members of Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) marched towards police barricades erected at Ferozeshah Road.Following an unsuccessful attempt to breach them, the students staged a sit-in — waving flags, raising slogans and holding up posters for 30 minutes — before security personnel detained them and took them to waiting buses.Rohan, a protester who came from Bengaluru to express solidarity with the agitation, said, “This protest is symbolic. You may think police are overpowering us, but we need to continue the struggle as there are millions who support us. One day, either the people or the oppressors will lose.” He hoped the latter would go down first.A few minutes after Ferozeshah Road was cleared out, members of Indian Youth Congress started marching from their office on Raisina Road towards Jantar Mantar. Walking towards security personnel, a protester said she wasn’t afraid of cops using force or detaining her as she was a “Gandhivaadi”.The protesters were allowed to march till Parliament Street police station, from where security personnel shoved them into buses to be taken away as prohibitory orders under Section 163 of BNSS were imposed there.An agitator said govt’s duty was to listen to people, not suppress them.
